whatItMeans.amber: Food-at-home prices are rising faster than the Fed’s 2% comfort zone.
whatItMeans.red: Grocery prices are rising fast: the last 3 months are running at a high annual pace.

familyImpact.amber: Your weekly grocery bill is creeping up. Staples you buy every week feel it first.
familyImpact.red: Food is taking a noticeably bigger share of the budget, and prices rarely fall back quickly.

whatToDo.amber: Buy an extra week of the shelf-stable food you already eat while prices are lower.
whatToDo.red: Build a 2–4 week pantry of staples you actually use, and switch to store brands where you can.

peripheralImpacts: Pet food and baby formula costs rise

whatItMeans.amber: Gas is above $4 a gallon on average nationwide.
whatItMeans.red: Gas is near record territory; the 2022 peak was about $5.

familyImpact.amber: Commuting and errands cost more each week, and delivery fees tend to follow.
familyImpact.red: Fuel is a real budget line now. Price spikes can also bring short local shortages.

whatToDo.amber: Keep the tank above half and combine trips. Check if your card or grocer offers fuel discounts.
whatToDo.red: Keep the tank above half, store fuel only in approved cans, and ask about remote-work days.

whatItMeans.amber: Crude oil is expensive, which usually means supply is tight somewhere in the world.
whatItMeans.red: Crude oil is at crisis-level prices, typically a sign of conflict or a supply disruption.

familyImpact.amber: Gas and heating oil prices tend to follow crude within a few weeks.
familyImpact.red: Expect higher prices for gas, heating oil, flights and shipped goods over the next 1–2 months.

whatToDo.amber: If you heat with oil or propane, price out a fill now rather than in winter.
whatToDo.red: Lock in heating fuel if you can, keep the car tank above half, and trim nonessential driving.

whatItMeans.amber: 30-year mortgage rates are above 7%.
whatItMeans.red: Mortgage rates are above 8.5%, higher than any time since 2000.

familyImpact.amber: Buying or refinancing costs more each month. Home equity lines get pricier too.
familyImpact.red: Moving or refinancing is very expensive, and adjustable-rate loans reset higher.

whatToDo.amber: If you have an adjustable-rate loan or HELOC, check when it resets.
whatToDo.red: Avoid new variable-rate debt. If you’re buying, get a rate lock in writing.

whatItMeans.amber: More homeowners are falling behind on mortgage payments than usual.
whatItMeans.red: Mortgage delinquencies are high, a sign of broad household financial stress.

familyImpact.amber: A sign that household budgets are stretched in many places.
familyImpact.red: Local home prices can soften and lenders get stricter with credit.

whatToDo.amber: Make sure you have at least a month of mortgage or rent set aside.
whatToDo.red: If a payment could be tight, call your lender before you miss it; options shrink after.

whatItMeans.amber: New unemployment claims are rising, meaning layoffs are picking up.
whatItMeans.red: Unemployment claims are at recession levels.

familyImpact.amber: Hiring slows and job security gets shakier, especially in cyclical industries.
familyImpact.red: Layoffs are widespread. Finding a new job may take months, not weeks.

whatToDo.amber: Update your resume and LinkedIn, and aim for 3 months of expenses in savings.
whatToDo.red: Build toward 6 months of expenses, pause big purchases, and know your state’s unemployment filing steps.

whatItMeans.amber: The economy is growing slowly, below its usual 2% pace.
whatItMeans.red: The economy shrank last quarter.

familyImpact.amber: Slow growth usually means slower hiring and smaller raises.
familyImpact.red: Recessions bring layoffs and tighter credit, usually for several quarters.

whatToDo.amber: Good time to build savings and pay down high-interest debt.
whatToDo.red: Hold off on big new debt and keep 3–6 months of expenses in cash.

whatItMeans.amber: The 10-year Treasury yield is swinging more than usual within a day.
whatItMeans.red: Bond markets are swinging as hard as in past crises such as March 2020 and the 2023 bank failures.

familyImpact.amber: Retirement balances may move more than usual. Nothing to act on by itself.
familyImpact.red: Loan rates can jump quickly and investment balances may drop sharply.

whatToDo.amber: No action needed. Avoid checking your 401k daily.
whatToDo.red: Don’t panic-sell. Make sure you have a few weeks of cash outside investments.

whatItMeans.amber: Demand at the latest 10-year Treasury auction was weaker than usual.
whatItMeans.red: Demand for US government debt was very weak at the latest auction.

familyImpact.amber: Weak demand can nudge up rates on mortgages and car loans.
familyImpact.red: Borrowing costs across the economy can rise quickly after weak auctions.

whatToDo.amber: If you’re about to borrow, consider locking a rate sooner rather than later.
whatToDo.red: Avoid new variable-rate debt and keep some cash outside the market.

whatItMeans.amber: More banks than usual have failed in the past year.
whatItMeans.red: Bank failures are running at a pace not seen since the 2008–2012 crisis.

familyImpact.amber: Insured deposits are safe up to $250K, but a failure can pause access for a day or two.
familyImpact.red: Short delays accessing money are possible if your bank is taken over.

whatToDo.amber: Check that your balances at each bank are under FDIC limits.
whatToDo.red: Keep accounts at two different banks and a few hundred dollars in cash at home.

whatItMeans.amber: Banks are borrowing more from the Fed’s emergency window than usual.
whatItMeans.red: Banks are leaning heavily on emergency Fed loans, as they did in March 2023.

familyImpact.amber: An early sign some banks need cash. Deposits under $250K remain insured.
familyImpact.red: Some banks are under real funding stress. Access delays are possible at weak banks.

whatToDo.amber: Confirm your deposits are within FDIC limits.
whatToDo.red: Spread savings across two banks and keep a small cash reserve at home.

whatItMeans.amber: Money is flowing out of US banks faster than normal this week.
whatItMeans.red: Deposits dropped as sharply as during the 2023 bank runs.

familyImpact.amber: Usually harmless on its own, but worth watching with other bank signals.
familyImpact.red: Banks under pressure may restrict withdrawals or tighten lending.

whatToDo.amber: No action needed beyond keeping deposits within FDIC limits.
whatToDo.red: Keep a few hundred dollars in cash and accounts at two banks.

whatItMeans.amber: The national emergency oil reserve is low compared with its history.
whatItMeans.red: The emergency oil reserve is at a multi-decade low.

familyImpact.amber: Less cushion if an oil shock hits, so price spikes could last longer.
familyImpact.red: The government has little room to calm a fuel price spike.

whatToDo.amber: No direct action; watch gas and crude prices.
whatToDo.red: Keep the car tank above half and heating fuel topped up ahead of winter.

whatItMeans.amber: Natural gas in storage is below the 5-year average.
whatItMeans.red: Gas storage is well below normal going into heating season.

familyImpact.amber: Heating and electric bills may run higher this winter.
familyImpact.red: Expect noticeably higher winter heating bills; cold snaps can strain supply.

whatToDo.amber: Ask your utility about budget billing, and seal drafty windows and doors.
whatToDo.red: Get a furnace check, weatherproof now, and have warm bedding and a safe backup heat plan.

whatItMeans.amber: Shipping a container across the ocean costs about twice the pre-2020 norm.
whatItMeans.red: Container shipping costs have spiked, as in the 2021 supply crunch.

familyImpact.amber: Imported goods get a bit pricier over the next 2–3 months.
familyImpact.red: Expect higher prices and some empty shelves for imported goods in 2–3 months.

whatToDo.amber: Buy planned imported items (electronics, appliances) sooner rather than later.
whatToDo.red: Buy needed imported goods, replacement parts and gifts early.

whatItMeans.amber: More drugs than usual are on the FDA’s shortage list.
whatItMeans.red: Drug shortages are widespread, near record levels.

familyImpact.amber: Some prescriptions may take longer to fill or need a substitute.
familyImpact.red: Common prescriptions may be hard to get for weeks at a time.

whatToDo.amber: Refill prescriptions a week early, and check the FDA list for your family’s medicines.
whatToDo.red: Ask your doctor about 90-day supplies and approved alternatives for critical medicines.

whatItMeans.amber: Attackers are actively using more newly found software flaws than usual.
whatItMeans.red: An unusually high number of flaws are being exploited in the wild right now.

familyImpact.amber: Phones, routers and apps you use may have flaws being exploited today.
familyImpact.red: Higher odds of outages or breaches at banks, hospitals and utilities.

whatToDo.amber: Install pending updates on phones, computers and your router this week.
whatToDo.red: Update everything now, turn on two-factor login for email and banking, and save key documents offline.

whatItMeans.amber: Several extreme weather alerts are active across the US right now.
whatItMeans.red: Many extreme weather alerts are active at once, e.g. hurricanes or tornado outbreaks.

familyImpact.amber: Check whether any alert covers your area or family members.
familyImpact.red: Large areas may lose power or road access; supplies can sell out ahead of storms.

whatToDo.amber: Check weather.gov for your area and charge your power banks.
whatToDo.red: If you’re in an affected area, follow local officials, fill water containers and fuel the car now.

whatItMeans.amber: FEMA has declared more disasters than usual in the last 90 days.
whatItMeans.red: An exceptionally high number of disasters have been declared recently.

familyImpact.amber: Federal help is spread across many places; response times can slow.
familyImpact.red: If disaster hits you now, expect to rely on your own supplies longer.

whatToDo.amber: Make sure you have 3 days of water, food and medicine at home.
whatToDo.red: Plan to be self-sufficient for a week: water, food, medicine, cash and a battery radio.

whatItMeans.amber: More countries than usual carry a “Do Not Travel” warning.
whatItMeans.red: An unusually large number of countries are under “Do Not Travel” warnings.

familyImpact.amber: International trips carry more risk of disruption.
familyImpact.red: Global instability is widespread; trips abroad can be cut short.

whatToDo.amber: Check passports are valid for 6+ months and enroll trips in the State Dept’s STEP program.
whatToDo.red: Reconsider nonessential travel abroad and keep passports current for the whole family.

whatItMeans.amber: Far fewer people are flying than normal.
whatItMeans.red: Air travel has collapsed, as it did in spring 2020.

familyImpact.amber: Something is keeping people home: an outbreak, a security event or economic stress.
familyImpact.red: Travel is disrupted nationwide; expect wider disruption to follow.

whatToDo.amber: Look at the other signals to see what’s driving it.
whatToDo.red: Postpone nonessential travel and check that home supplies cover 2 weeks.

whatItMeans.amber: Rents are rising faster than usual compared with a year ago.
whatItMeans.red: Rents are rising very fast, close to the 2023 peak.

familyImpact.amber: Expect a bigger increase at your next lease renewal.
familyImpact.red: Lease renewals may come with steep increases, and cheaper places get scarce.

whatToDo.amber: Check your lease end date and start looking at what similar places rent for nearby.
whatToDo.red: Talk to your landlord early about renewal terms, and call a free housing counselor if the numbers don’t work.

whatItMeans.amber: Electricity prices are up noticeably from a year ago.
whatItMeans.red: Electricity prices are rising very fast, near the 2022 spike.

familyImpact.amber: Your monthly electric bill is likely higher than last year.
familyImpact.red: Electric bills are a real strain; falling behind can lead to shutoff notices.

whatToDo.amber: Ask your utility about budget billing so the bill stays the same each month.
whatToDo.red: Apply for heating and cooling help (LIHEAP) and ask your utility about payment plans before you fall behind.

whatItMeans.amber: Car insurance prices are up sharply from a year ago.
whatItMeans.red: Car insurance prices are rising at a near-record pace.

familyImpact.amber: Expect a higher premium at your next renewal.
familyImpact.red: Renewals may jump a lot; that’s money out of every paycheck for anyone who drives to work.

whatToDo.amber: Get two or three quotes before your policy renews; switching often saves money.
whatToDo.red: Shop quotes now and ask about higher deductibles or usage-based discounts.

cost_auto_insurance.dataPointLabel: Car insurance vs a year ago

whatItMeans.amber: Day care and preschool prices are rising faster than usual.
whatItMeans.red: Childcare prices are rising at a record pace.

familyImpact.amber: Childcare may cost more at your next enrollment or renewal.
familyImpact.red: Higher childcare costs can make working hours harder to cover.

whatToDo.amber: Ask your provider about any planned increases and check if your employer has a dependent care account.
whatToDo.red: Check your state’s childcare assistance through 211, and use a dependent care account if your job offers one.

whatItMeans.amber: More people are staying on unemployment longer, so jobs are harder to find.
whatItMeans.red: Finding a new job is taking much longer than usual.

familyImpact.amber: If you lost work, it could take longer to replace the income.
familyImpact.red: A job loss now could mean months without a paycheck.

whatToDo.amber: Build toward three months of expenses and keep your resume current.
whatToDo.red: Know how to file for unemployment in your state, and pause big new debts.

whatItMeans.amber: Typical paychecks are falling behind rising prices.
whatItMeans.red: Paychecks are losing ground to prices quickly.

familyImpact.amber: The same paycheck buys a little less than last year.
familyImpact.red: Real income is shrinking; budgets that worked last year may not now.

whatToDo.amber: Check you’re getting every credit you qualify for, like the earned income tax credit.
whatToDo.red: Review your budget for the biggest bills, and check benefits like SNAP and Lifeline you may now qualify for.

job_03_real_wages.dataPointLabel: Pay vs prices, a year apart

whatItMeans.amber: Unemployment is starting to rise above its recent low.
whatItMeans.red: Unemployment has risen enough that a recession has usually already begun.

familyImpact.amber: Hiring may slow over the coming months.
familyImpact.red: Layoffs tend to spread across industries during recessions.

whatToDo.amber: Put a little more into savings each paycheck while you can.
whatToDo.red: Aim for several months of expenses in cash and hold off on big new debt.

whatItMeans.amber: More families are falling behind on credit card payments.
whatItMeans.red: Credit card late payments are at levels last seen in serious downturns.

familyImpact.amber: Banks may tighten credit limits and approvals.
familyImpact.red: Credit gets harder to get just when people need it most.

whatToDo.amber: Pay more than the minimum on your highest-rate card, and don’t rely on cards as your emergency fund.
whatToDo.red: If payments are slipping, call your card company before you miss one, or talk to a free credit counselor.

whatItMeans.amber: Virus levels in sewage are high in many places, so a wave of illness is likely.
whatItMeans.red: Virus levels are high across most of the country.

familyImpact.amber: Sick days and school absences are more likely in the coming weeks.
familyImpact.red: Expect a lot of illness at work and school; plan for missed days.

whatToDo.amber: Restock fever reducer, tests and tissues, and check you’re up to date on vaccines.
whatToDo.red: Line up backup childcare and know your sick-leave options before someone gets sick.

whatItMeans.amber: Measles cases are running well above a normal year's pace.
whatItMeans.red: Measles is spreading widely: more cases in four weeks than in most full years.

familyImpact.amber: Babies under a year and anyone unvaccinated are most at risk. Outbreaks can close schools and daycares.
familyImpact.red: Exposed children without two MMR doses can be kept out of school or daycare for up to 21 days.

whatToDo.amber: Check that everyone's measles shots (MMR) are up to date. Your doctor or your state's immunization record can tell you.
whatToDo.red: Confirm everyone's MMR shots this week. Ask your doctor about an early dose for a baby 6 to 11 months old before international travel.

whatItMeans.amber: Unemployment for 20- to 24-year-olds is above its usual range. New grads are having a harder time getting hired.
whatItMeans.red: Young workers are being shut out: entry-level hiring has dropped sharply.

familyImpact.amber: Grown kids, new grads and entry-level workers take longer to find a first job. Weekly jobless claims miss them, because many never qualified for benefits.
familyImpact.red: Young adults may need family support for longer. First jobs and internships get scarce.

whatToDo.amber: If someone in the house is job hunting, start early and apply widely. Your state's job center lists free training programs.
whatToDo.red: Plan for a longer job search for young adults in the house, and look at your state's apprenticeship and training programs.

whatItMeans.amber: Doctor, hospital, insurance and drug prices are rising faster than usual.
whatItMeans.red: Medical prices are rising at a pace not seen in over 20 years.

familyImpact.amber: Copays, prescriptions and premiums tend to follow at your next renewal.
familyImpact.red: Health costs take a bigger bite, especially on high-deductible plans.

whatToDo.amber: At open enrollment, compare plans on total yearly cost (premium plus deductible), not the premium alone.
whatToDo.red: Ask for generic drugs and 90-day supplies, and use your plan's price tool before non-urgent care.

whatItMeans.amber: Investors want extra interest to hold long-term US debt. That keeps mortgage and loan rates up.
whatItMeans.red: The extra interest investors demand for long-term US debt is near its highest this century.

familyImpact.amber: Mortgage and car-loan rates can stay high even if the Fed cuts.
familyImpact.red: Borrowing stays expensive for longer, and refinancing gets harder.

whatToDo.amber: If you plan to borrow for a home or car this year, get rate quotes early and ask about locking a rate.
whatToDo.red: Pay down variable-rate debt first, and don't build plans around rates falling soon.

peripheralImpacts: Car loan and credit card rates

whatItMeans.amber: Americans feel worse about the economy than usual.
whatItMeans.red: National mood is near its record low.

familyImpact.amber: Mood often reads worse than the hard numbers, and since 2022 it moves with politics.
familyImpact.red: Gloom spreads through news and feeds faster than the economy changes.

whatToDo.amber: Compare with your own costs, income and credit on this page before changing plans.
whatToDo.red: Don't make a big move you can't undo because of the national mood. Act on your own numbers.

whatItMeans.amber: Employers are hiring at one of the slowest rates in a decade, even though layoffs are low.
whatItMeans.red: Hiring has nearly frozen, close to the 2009 low.

familyImpact.amber: If someone in the house loses a job, the next one may take months to find.
familyImpact.red: A job search could take much longer than usual, especially for entry-level and office roles.

whatToDo.amber: Keep your résumé current and stay in touch with people in your field. Aim for six months of expenses saved if one income is at risk.
whatToDo.red: Build savings toward nine to twelve months of essential costs, and cut fixed bills where you can.

job_06_hires_rate.dataPointLabel: Hires as a share of jobs

whatItMeans.amber: Big tech stocks are down 20% or more from their high, a bear market for the companies that dominate index funds.
whatItMeans.red: Tech stocks have fallen 35% or more, the size of the 2022 drop and the line for an AI-linked bust.

familyImpact.amber: Retirement and index-fund balances drop, because a handful of tech companies make up a large share of the S&P 500.
familyImpact.red: 401(k) balances fall sharply, and tech-sector layoffs usually follow.

whatToDo.amber: Don't sell in a panic. Check how much of your savings rides on a few tech stocks, and keep money you need soon in cash or Treasury bills.
whatToDo.red: Don't sell in a panic; past drops recovered, sometimes over years. Keep 6 to 12 months of expenses outside stocks.

whatItMeans.amber: The State Department now says to reconsider travel to China.
whatItMeans.red: The State Department says do not travel to China. At 5 it has ordered US staff or families out.

familyImpact.amber: Tension with China raises the chance of trade cutoffs, electronics shortages and cyberattacks on US utilities.
familyImpact.red: Expect supply shocks in electronics and generic medicines within weeks to months.

whatToDo.amber: Check passport dates for everyone, and buy any electronics you were already planning to buy.
whatToDo.red: Refill key prescriptions to 90 days where allowed, keep 2 to 4 weeks of cash at home, and confirm your backups work.

whatItMeans.amber: The State Department raised Taiwan's travel advisory above normal, which is rare.
whatItMeans.red: The State Department says to reconsider travel to Taiwan or worse. At 5 it has ordered US staff or families out.

familyImpact.amber: Taiwan makes most of the world's advanced chips. Pressure on it shows up first in electronics prices and the stock market.
familyImpact.red: A blockade would hit electronics, medicines and shipping within weeks, and could bring cyberattacks on US utilities.

whatToDo.amber: Check passport dates, and buy planned electronics sooner rather than later.
whatToDo.red: Refill key prescriptions to 90 days where allowed, build food staples toward 30 days, keep 2 to 4 weeks of cash, and charge backup batteries.

whatItMeans.amber: Electricity prices are rising at least 2 points faster than prices overall.
whatItMeans.red: Electric bills are outpacing inflation by 4 points or more.

familyImpact.amber: Power takes a bigger bite each month, and summer and winter bills hit hardest.
familyImpact.red: Utility bills are becoming a real budget problem, and rate increases tend to stick.

whatToDo.amber: Ask your utility about budget billing, and check your state utility commission for pending rate increases.
whatToDo.red: Look at efficiency upgrades that pay back quickly (thermostat, insulation, LED lighting) and any state bill-assistance programs.
